learn.canDo: Explain what temperature, top-p, and top-k do to the next-token choice, and set them for extraction versus brainstorming.
learn.why: The same prompt giving different answers confuses every team once. Knowing the sampler is the difference between flaky tests and a controlled feature.
learn.keyIdea: Temperature adds probability to the unlikely.

learn.canDo: Explain why models fabricate when knowledge runs out, and layer retrieval, abstention, citation, and verification against it.
learn.why: A confident wrong answer in production is a refund, a legal issue, or a lost customer. Defending against it is the first question in any AI interview.
learn.keyIdea: Plausible is not the same as true.

learn.canDo: Separate prefill delay from decode speed, and fix a slow response with streaming, caching, shorter prompts, or a smaller model.
learn.why: Users judge an AI feature by how soon it starts and how long it takes. The two delays have different causes and different fixes.
learn.keyIdea: Prefill sets the first token; decode sets the rest.

learn.canDo: Estimate an LLM feature's monthly bill from traffic and tokens, and cut it with caching, routing, and batching.
learn.why: The AI line item is often the fastest-growing cost in a product. Doing the arithmetic aloud is expected in AI-engineering interviews.
learn.keyIdea: Requests × tokens × price, split input and output.

chapter.story: The demo goes well. Then Pigeon Copilot meets real users, real traffic, and a real invoice.
outcomes: Control sampling for stable or creative output
Separate time to first token from output speed
Estimate and cut an LLM bill
chapter.why: Everything that goes wrong after a demo is a behaviour of the model under real conditions: variation, fabrication, delay, and cost. This chapter makes each of those a number you can reason about.
chapter.payoff: You can explain why outputs vary, how to keep a bot honest, why a response feels slow, and what a feature will cost, which are the first questions in an AI-engineering interview.
